title: A maximal-torus centralizer lies in every Borel subgroup through the torus
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$, and all subgroup schemes are closed [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness is as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] and connectedness as in [def-weil-connected-scheme]; geometrically connected means connected after extension to an algebraic closure $\bar k$. A torus is a group scheme $T$ with $T_{\bar k}\simeq(\mathbf G_m)^r$ for some integer $r\geq0$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. A Borel subgroup of $G$ is a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup, where solvable means that successive commutator subgroup schemes eventually become trivial. A maximal torus is a torus not strictly contained in another torus subgroup. For a subgroup $H\subseteq G$, its centralizer functor is $C_G(H)(A)=\{g\in G(A):g_{A\prime}h=hg_{A\prime}\text{ for every commutative }A\text{-algebra }A\prime\text{ and every }h\in H(A\prime)\}$. Assume that $k$ is algebraically closed, $G$ is smooth and connected, $T\subseteq G$ is a maximal torus, and $B\subseteq G$ is any Borel subgroup containing $T$. Then $C_G(T)\subseteq B$ as subgroup functors: for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and every $g\in C_G(T)(A)$, one has $g\in B(A)$.

source.place: Corollary 17.39(b), printed p.364; the proof invokes Corollaries 12.40 and 17.29. Only (b) is stated here, with the stronger base-field restriction needed by the parent proof.

proof.text: Put $C=C_G(T)$. By [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-smooth-connected], $C$ is a smooth connected closed subgroup scheme of $G$: over the algebraically closed field $k$ the geometric connectedness hypothesis on $G$ is its assumed connectedness. Since $T$ is commutative, $T\subseteq C$. For every $k$-algebra $A$, every point of $C(A)$ commutes with every point of $T(A)$, so $T$ is central in $C$. Any torus of $C$ properly containing $T$ would also be a torus of $G$ properly containing $T$. Thus $T$ is a maximal torus of $C$.
Apply [lem-sfb-central-maximal-torus-nilpotent] to the smooth connected affine group $C$ and its central maximal torus $T$. It follows that $C$ is solvable.

source.place: Proposition 17.23 and the proof of Corollary 17.29, pp.359--360.

proof.text: Among smooth connected solvable closed subgroups of $G$ containing $C$, choose $B_0$ with greatest dimension. The collection is nonempty because it contains $C$; its dimensions are nonnegative integers bounded by $\dim G$, by [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products]. The same cited statement says every proper closed inclusion of smooth connected group schemes strictly increases dimension. Consequently no smooth connected solvable subgroup can properly contain $B_0$. By the definition of Borel subgroup, $B_0$ is a Borel subgroup of $G$, and $T\subseteq C\subseteq B_0$.

source.place: Definition 17.6 and the following paragraph, pp.353--354; proof of Corollary 17.29, p.360.

proof.text: Both $B_0$ and the prescribed $B$ contain the maximal torus $T$. By [lem-sfb-torus-normalizer-borel-transitivity], choose $n\in G(k)$ such that $nTn^{-1}=T$ and $nB_0n^{-1}=B$ as subgroup schemes.

source.place: Corollary 17.11, p.355, as applied in Corollary 17.29, p.360.

proof.text: Fix any commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and $c\in C(A)$. For every commutative $A$-algebra $A\prime$ and $t\in T(A\prime)$, the element $n_{A\prime}tn_{A\prime}^{-1}$ belongs to $T(A\prime)$, so it commutes with $c_{A\prime}$. Multiplying this identity by $n_{A\prime}^{-1}$ on the left and by $n_{A\prime}$ on the right shows that $n_A^{-1}cn_A$ belongs to $C(A)$. Since $C\subseteq B_0$, this point belongs to $B_0(A)$, and hence $c\in n_AB_0(A)n_A^{-1}=B(A)$. This proves the desired containment on every algebra, including nonreduced algebras.
